extracted.intended_audience: aspiring short-story writers and creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing effective short stories, focused on economy, character, plot shape, and reader engagement, drawn from Kurt Vonnegut's eight rules and accompanying notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the time of a total stranger in such a way that he or she will not feel the time was wasted.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the time of a total stranger in such a way that he or she will not feel the time was wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle of respect for the reader's time; ensure the story justifies the investment of attention. No additional examples on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the reader at least one character he or she can root for.
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the reader at least one character he or she can root for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages empathetic or sympathetic figures so readers care about outcomes; implies inclusion of at least one accessible point of engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every character should want something, even if it is only a glass of water.
rubrics_metrics.description: Every character should want something, even if it is only a glass of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drive characters with desires or needs—big or small—to create motivation and forward momentum; even trivial wants count as valid motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every sentence must do one of two things — reveal character or advance the action.
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sentence must do one of two things — reveal character or advance the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strict economy rule: avoid sentences that are merely decorative or expository without serving character revelation or plot movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start as close to the end as possible.
rubrics_metrics.description: Start as close to the end as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the story near the resolution or climax to maintain narrative economy and avoid unnecessary setup; favor immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a sadist. Make awful things happen to characters so the reader may see what they are made of.
rubrics_metrics.description: Be a sadist. No matter how sweet and innocent your leading characters, make awful things happen to them — in order that the reader may see what they are made of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce adversity and testing; conflict reveals character and creates stakes. The page frames this as necessary to expose true character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to please just one person.
rubrics_metrics.description: Write to please just one person. If you open a window and make love to the world, so to speak, your story will get pneumonia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the story toward a specific reader or sensibility rather than trying to please everyone; warns against diluting voice/intent by pandering to a broad audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give your readers as much information as possible as soon as possible; to heck with suspense.
rubrics_metrics.description: Give your readers as much information as possible as soon as possible. To heck with suspense. Readers should have such complete understanding of what is going on, where and why, that they could finish the story themselves, should cockroaches eat the last few pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity and reader understanding over withholding information for suspense; provide context and facts early so readers comprehend the situation fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vonnegut's caveat about rule exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut notes that Flannery O'Connor broke practically every one of his rules but the first; great writers tend to do that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules are guidelines, not absolute laws. Exceptional writers may successfully break many rules; use judgment and learn the rules before subverting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories follow recognizable 'shapes' (plot arcs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories follow plottable arcs of fortune (Man in Hole, Boy Meets Girl, Cinderella, etc.). The shape itself is part of why a story works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the macro-shape or arc of the story—common plot contours help produce satisfying narratives. Use shape deliberately as part of craft.
